The Battle of Vicksburg. A pivotal American Civil War siege fought from May eighteenth to July fourth, eighteen sixty-three, in which Union forces under Ulysses S. Grant besieged and captured the Confederate stronghold of Vicksburg, Mississippi. The victory gave the North control of the Mississippi River, split the Confederacy in two, and proved Grant's military genius, marking a decisive turning point toward Union victory.

The battle climaxed on the Fourth of July with Confederate surrender, yielding a psychological victory on American independence day. It was part of Grant's larger Vicksburg Campaign, which spanned from December eighteen sixty-two to July eighteen sixty-three and involved feints, river operations coordinated with the United States Navy, and forced marches through Mississippi's difficult terrain.

The siege lasted forty-seven days of relentless bombardment. Union forces surrounded the city from all sides while Confederates faced starvation, disease, and dwindling ammunition supplies. Some soldiers ate mules and dogs to survive. The same week, the Battle of Gettysburg concluded in Pennsylvania from July first to third. These two victories, Vicksburg and Gettysburg, marked a strategic turning point indicating the North's military ascendancy.

Vicksburg was the last Confederate stronghold on the Mississippi River. Its capture gave the Union complete control of the entire river, effectively splitting Texas, Arkansas, and Louisiana from the Eastern Confederacy. Grant's campaign pioneered a radical logistical innovation called living off the land, moving without supply lines and foraging from the countryside to maintain mobility and speed. This tactic would foreshadow General Sherman's later March to the Sea.

The battle established Ulysses S. Grant as the North's most strategically capable field general. President Lincoln recognized his talent and promoted him to Commanding General of all Union armies in eighteen sixty-four. Approximately ten thousand Confederate prisoners were captured, while Union casualties totaled around ten thousand killed, wounded, or missing. Confederate attempts at relief by General Joe Johnston failed. Vicksburg's fall demoralized the South and demonstrated Union capacity for coordinated strategy, marking the beginning of the Confederacy's military decline.
